title: Type 2 Diabetes: Confirm the Diagnosis, Then Treat Risk and Glycemia Together
bottomLine: Type 2 diabetes diagnosis uses validated Canadian criteria and confirmation when the patient is asymptomatic. Initial management is not 'metformin and wait': classify the presentation, identify metabolic decompensation, set an individualized glycemic target, and treat cardiovascular, kidney and weight-related risk alongside glucose.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, blurred vision and recurrent infection suggest symptomatic hyperglycemia.
Heart failure, CKD and established/high cardiovascular risk can change first-line medication selection independent of A1C.
differentiate: Ketosis, rapid weight loss, autoimmune history or severe insulin deficiency should prompt reconsideration of type 1/LADA rather than assuming routine type 2 diabetes.
Stress hyperglycemia during acute illness is not automatically chronic diabetes.
assessment: Assess symptoms, weight trajectory, pregnancy, medications, renal function, cardiovascular/renal disease, hypoglycemia risk, food/medication access and patient goals.
Screen baseline BP, smoking, feet/neuropathy and other complication risks as appropriate.
workup: Use A1C and/or plasma glucose diagnostic criteria and confirm an isolated abnormal result when the patient is asymptomatic.
Use ketones/electrolytes/acid-base evaluation urgently when metabolic decompensation is possible.
management: Provide diabetes self-management support, nutrition/activity counselling and pharmacotherapy matched to glycemia plus cardiorenal indications.
Start insulin promptly when severe symptomatic hyperglycemia or metabolic decompensation is present rather than waiting for oral therapy to fail.
medicationSafety: Choose therapy using renal function, hypoglycemia risk, pregnancy, interactions, cost and cardiorenal benefit.
SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/peri-procedural education because euglycemic DKA can occur.
redFlags: Unintentional weight loss with marked hyperglycemia
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and explain that medication choice may be driven by heart/kidney protection even when A1C is near target.
followUp: Reassess glycemia, adverse effects, adherence/access and cardiorenal risk after treatment starts or changes.
examTrap: Delaying insulin in metabolic decompensation because the patient has presumed type 2 diabetes—or choosing therapy from A1C alone while ignoring CKD/HF.
oneLinePearl: Diagnose correctly, then treat the person's metabolic and cardiorenal risk—not just the A1C.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Adults — 2024 Update

title: Type 1 Diabetes: Basal Insulin Is Continuous Physiology
bottomLine: Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency. Use a basal-bolus or pump strategy that provides continuous basal insulin plus prandial/correction coverage; fasting or NPO status may change doses but does not remove the need for basal insulin because interruption can precipitate DKA quickly.
recognize: Insulin needs vary with meals, activity, illness, pregnancy and the honeymoon phase.
Pump interruption can produce rapid insulin deficiency because there is no long-acting depot.
differentiate: Basal insulin covers background hepatic glucose production; prandial insulin covers food; correction insulin treats above-target glucose.
Holding prandial insulin for a missed meal is not the same as holding basal insulin.
assessment: Review CGM/SMBG patterns, hypoglycemia, meal timing/carbohydrate strategy, exercise, injection/pump sites, adherence, sick-day plan and psychosocial burden.
workup: Use A1C plus glucose/CGM metrics for longitudinal control and ketone testing during significant hyperglycemia or illness when appropriate.
Evaluate recurrent unexplained variability for insulin timing, technique, site, pump/set, food, exercise or endocrine contributors.
management: Individualize basal-bolus or pump therapy with carbohydrate/prandial and correction planning.
Ensure backup insulin plans for pump failure and adequate education before major regimen changes.
medicationSafety: Never omit all basal insulin in type 1 diabetes unless another clinician-directed insulin replacement strategy is active.
Match concentrated insulin/device use exactly to the prescribed product and delivery device.
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, ketone checks, hypoglycemia rescue and pump-failure backup.
Driving/exercise plans must account for hypoglycemia risk.
followUp: Review patterns rather than isolated values and adjust one component of the regimen according to when hyper/hypoglycemia occurs.
examTrap: Holding all insulin because a person with type 1 diabetes is NPO.
oneLinePearl: No food changes prandial insulin; it does not erase basal insulin physiology.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes

title: Diabetes Medications Beyond Metformin: Choose for the Patient, Not the Drug List
bottomLine: After or alongside metformin, medication choice is driven by cardiorenal disease, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, renal function, adverse effects, access and patient preference. Specific SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists may be indicated for heart/kidney benefit even when additional A1C lowering is not the main need.
recognize: HF/CKD/ASCVD risk can make SGLT2 or GLP-1 therapy high-value independent of glucose target.
Insulin and sulfonylureas have greater hypoglycemia risk than most newer noninsulin classes.
differentiate: DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are not routinely combined because the mechanism/benefit overlap adds little value.
Medication intensification is not always appropriate in frail patients with recurrent hypoglycemia.
assessment: Assess eGFR, HF/ASCVD/CKD, weight goals, hypoglycemia history, GI disease, infection risk, cost/coverage, injection preference, pregnancy and current medications.
workup: Use A1C/glucose patterns plus renal/other class-specific monitoring rather than a universal lab panel for every drug.
Reassess why target is not met before adding medication: adherence, side effects, food insecurity, steroids or wrong diagnosis may matter.
management: Select and sequence therapy using current Diabetes Canada cardiorenal/glycemic guidance and patient goals.
De-intensify when treatment burden/hypoglycemia risk exceeds expected benefit.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors: volume/genital infection/euglycemic-DKA considerations and temporary holds in major illness/prolonged fasting as appropriate.
GLP-1 therapy: GI tolerance, gallbladder/pancreatitis symptoms and product-specific contraindications.
counselling: Explain the expected benefit of each drug in terms of glucose, heart, kidney, weight and adverse effects.
Review sick-day rules only for medications where they apply.
followUp: Reassess tolerability, glucose/A1C, kidney function and the clinical outcome the drug was chosen to improve.
examTrap: Refusing a cardiorenal-protective drug because A1C is already at target—or adding multiple drugs without reassessing recurrent hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: Beyond metformin, comorbidity and safety choose the drug as much as the A1C does.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Adults — 2024 Update
Diabetes Canada CKD in Diabetes — 2025 Update

title: Insulin Initiation and Titration: Match the Pattern Before Raising the Dose
bottomLine: Insulin titration should correct the glucose pattern that the insulin component actually influences. Basal insulin targets fasting/background hyperglycemia; prandial insulin targets meal excursions. Recurrent hypoglycemia or large basal doses with persistent post-meal hyperglycemia signal that simply increasing basal insulin is the wrong move.
recognize: Marked symptomatic hyperglycemia, ketosis or catabolic weight loss can require prompt insulin initiation.
Fasting-at-target with high postprandial values is not a reason to keep escalating basal insulin.
differentiate: Basal-only initiation in type 2 diabetes differs from basal-bolus treatment in type 1 or severe decompensation.
Correction insulin should not become the only long-term strategy when predictable basal/prandial needs are present.
assessment: Review fasting and meal-related glucose pattern, meals, hypoglycemia, renal function, weight, steroid timing, injection technique, access and ability to self-manage.
workup: Use SMBG/CGM at times that answer the titration question; do not collect random values without relating them to insulin timing and meals.
management: Start and titrate insulin using a validated patient-specific protocol and clear self-titration instructions when appropriate.
Add or redistribute prandial coverage when post-meal hyperglycemia persists despite appropriate fasting control rather than over-basalizing.
medicationSafety: Reduce/hold the responsible insulin component when clinically important hypoglycemia occurs and investigate the cause.
Renal decline, reduced intake and acute illness can sharply reduce insulin requirements.
redFlags: Cognitive/functional inability to use the prescribed regimen safely
counselling: Teach injection/device technique, hypoglycemia rescue, missed-meal rules, sick-day guidance and storage.
Make titration instructions numeric/clear enough to use safely rather than saying 'adjust as needed'.
followUp: Review the pattern within an appropriate interval after initiation/titration and simplify when regimen complexity exceeds safe self-management.
examTrap: Continuing to increase basal insulin when fasting glucose is controlled but post-meal glucose remains high and hypoglycemia is emerging.
oneLinePearl: Titrate the insulin that owns the glucose problem.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada pharmacologic glycemic management guidance

title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring: Read the Pattern, Not One Sensor Number
bottomLine: CGM interpretation is pattern recognition: time below range, time in range, time above range, variability and when excursions occur relative to insulin, meals, exercise and sleep. A single sensor reading—especially when symptoms do not match—should not trigger a major dose change without considering lag, compression, sensor error and confirmatory capillary glucose when appropriate.
recognize: Overnight/recurrent lows, post-meal spikes and exercise-related patterns reveal regimen problems that A1C can hide.
A1C and CGM can disagree when red-cell turnover or glycemic variability changes.
differentiate: Interstitial glucose can lag blood glucose during rapid change.
Compression lows or sensor failure can produce false readings; symptom discordance warrants verification according to device instructions.
assessment: Review wear time/data sufficiency, medication/insulin timing, meals, activity, alcohol, sleep, hypoglycemia awareness and device alerts.
workup: Use standardized CGM summaries/ambulatory glucose profiles when enough data are available and interpret trends across multiple days.
Confirm with capillary glucose when device guidance or clinical discordance requires it.
management: Prioritize reducing clinically important hypoglycemia before pursuing tighter average glucose.
Adjust the regimen component linked to the timing of the pattern and reassess after the change.
medicationSafety: Do not stack rapid insulin doses because CGM remains high before prior insulin has had time to act.
Set alert thresholds and escalation plans that the patient can respond to safely.
redFlags: Persistent high glucose with ketones in insulin-deficient patient
Sensor readings inconsistent with severe symptoms
counselling: Teach trend arrows, lag, compression/error, backup meter use and how to respond to alerts without panic dosing.
followUp: Review time-in-range/hypoglycemia/variability and functional burden after regimen/device changes.
examTrap: Giving repeated correction insulin from one rising CGM trend without considering active insulin and interstitial lag.
oneLinePearl: CGM is a movie; dose decisions should not be made from one frame.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada type 1 diabetes and glucose-monitoring resources

title: DKA: Treat Ketosis, Potassium, Volume, and the Cause
bottomLine: DKA is a ketoacidosis emergency caused by insulin deficiency, not simply a high-glucose emergency. Treat volume depletion, assess and replace potassium safely, provide insulin, monitor metabolic resolution and find the precipitating cause; normal or modest glucose does not exclude DKA, especially with pregnancy or SGLT2 inhibitor use.
recognize: Polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, tachypnea/Kussmaul breathing and altered mental status are common.
Euglycemic DKA can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors, fasting and pregnancy.
differentiate: HHS has more profound hyperosmolar dehydration and less prominent ketoacidosis.
Starvation/alcoholic ketosis and lactic acidosis can mimic parts of the picture.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, volume depletion, infection/ischemia symptoms, insulin omission/pump failure, pregnancy and SGLT2 exposure.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, renal function, acid-base assessment, beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones and anion-gap context; obtain cause-directed ECG/cultures/imaging as indicated.
management: Use an acute-care protocol with isotonic fluids, potassium-aware insulin and dextrose when needed to continue clearing ketosis.
Treat the precipitating cause and continue until ketoacidosis resolves rather than stopping when glucose normalizes.
medicationSafety: Insulin can rapidly worsen hypokalemia; do not start insulin blindly when potassium is dangerously low.
SGLT2-associated DKA may have less impressive hyperglycemia.
counselling: After recovery, teach sick-day rules, ketone testing, insulin continuity and SGLT2 hold rules when applicable.
followUp: Ensure insulin/access barriers, precipitating cause and diabetes follow-up are addressed before transition home.
examTrap: Stopping DKA treatment because glucose normalized while ketosis/acidosis persists—or missing DKA because glucose is not extremely high.
oneLinePearl: DKA resolution is about ketones/acidosis and safe electrolytes, not just the glucose value.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults

title: HHS: Hyperosmolar Dehydration Is the Core Emergency
bottomLine: HHS is profound hyperosmolar dehydration with severe hyperglycemia and neurologic risk, often with less ketoacidosis than DKA. Fluid resuscitation, electrolyte/osmolality monitoring, insulin timing and treatment of the precipitant require controlled correction because rapid shifts can cause harm.
recognize: Marked dehydration, weakness, hypotension, altered mental status and very high glucose/osmolality are typical.
Older adults may present after days of reduced intake, infection or medication disruption.
differentiate: DKA has more prominent ketosis/acidosis; mixed DKA/HHS occurs and should be recognized.
Stroke, sepsis and toxic/metabolic encephalopathy can coexist with or mimic HHS-related mental status change.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, volume deficit, urine output, infection/ischemia, medications and baseline renal/cardiac function.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, renal function, osmolality, ketones and acid-base data; evaluate precipitating infection, MI, stroke or medication causes based on presentation.
management: Use hospital protocol with careful isotonic fluid replacement, electrolyte management and insulin after initial resuscitation/according to physiology.
Correct hyperosmolality gradually while monitoring neurologic status and hemodynamics.
medicationSafety: Insulin and fluids shift potassium and osmolality; frequent monitoring is required.
Heart/kidney disease increases the hazard of indiscriminate large-volume resuscitation and requires reassessment.
counselling: After stabilization, review hydration access, sick-day plans and the medication/adherence issue that precipitated HHS.
followUp: Address cognitive/social barriers and arrange diabetes follow-up before discharge to prevent recurrence.
examTrap: Treating HHS as 'just high glucose' and rapidly driving glucose down without managing volume, electrolytes and osmolality.
oneLinePearl: HHS is primarily a hyperosmolar dehydration emergency; correction must be controlled.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults

title: Hypoglycemia: Treat the Low, Then Redesign the Risk
bottomLine: Hypoglycemia is both an acute treatment problem and a medication-safety signal. Correct the low promptly, then determine the cause and reduce recurrence by changing insulin/secretagogue exposure, meal/activity mismatch, kidney-related clearance, alcohol risk or unrealistic glycemic targets.
recognize: Autonomic symptoms include tremor, sweating and palpitations; neuroglycopenia causes confusion, behavioural change, seizure or coma.
Older/frail patients may present with falls or delirium rather than classic adrenergic symptoms.
differentiate: A conscious patient safe to swallow can use fast-acting carbohydrate; severe hypoglycemia requires external assistance with glucagon or IV glucose according to setting.
Persistent unexplained hypoglycemia without glucose-lowering drugs requires a separate endocrine/hepatic/critical-illness differential.
assessment: Confirm glucose promptly when feasible, assess airway/neurologic status and review insulin/secretagogues, meals, activity, alcohol, renal function, weight loss and food access.
workup: For recurrent episodes, use glucose/CGM patterns and medication timing; investigate non-diabetic/unexplained hypoglycemia only when a true low is documented in the appropriate clinical context.
management: Treat immediately using current Diabetes Canada hypoglycemia guidance and reassess after treatment.
Redesign the regimen/target after severe or recurrent episodes; consider glucagon prescription and technology support for high-risk patients.
medicationSafety: Renal decline can prolong insulin/secretagogue action.
Do not 'solve' recurrent hypoglycemia by telling the patient to eat extra calories around an unsafe medication regimen.
counselling: Teach fast-carbohydrate treatment, recheck timing, driving safety, glucagon and when emergency services are needed.
followUp: Any severe episode warrants prompt medication/target review with documented recurrence-prevention plan.
examTrap: Treating the glucose successfully and sending the patient home without changing the regimen that caused the episode.
oneLinePearl: The rescue ends the low; prevention ends the problem.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hypoglycemia in Adults — 2023 Update
